nodes.label: Identify angle types and pairs
nodes.description: Identify and name the types of angles (acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex, from a diagram or from its size in degrees) and the angle pairs (adjacent, vertically opposite, supplementary and complementary angles, and the corresponding, co-interior and alternate angles formed by a transversal) in a diagram, and use these names to fill in labelled angles.

nodes.label: Calculate angles with parallel lines
nodes.description: Calculate unknown angles in a diagram with parallel lines and a transversal, giving a reason for each step (corresponding, alternate, co-interior and vertically opposite angles, and angles on a straight line).

nodes.label: Determine whether lines are parallel
nodes.description: Determine whether two lines are parallel by testing whether corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior angles are equal or co-interior angles are supplementary, and explain why lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other.

nodes.label: Unknown angles and sides in triangles
nodes.description: Calculate unknown angles and side lengths in triangle figures, using the type of triangle (isosceles, equilateral, right-angled), the sum of the angles in a triangle (180°) and the theorem of Pythagoras.

nodes.label: Congruent triangles
nodes.description: Determine whether two triangles are congruent, state the rule (RHS, SSS, SAS or AAS) with the congruence written in the correct order of letters, and use congruent triangles to find unknown sides and angles.

nodes.label: Similar triangles
nodes.description: Identify which diagram gives a pair of similar triangles, using the AAA rule (equal corresponding angles) or the SSS rule (corresponding sides in proportion).

nodes.label: Properties of a parallelogram
nodes.description: Prove that the opposite sides and opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal and that its diagonals bisect each other, and use these properties to calculate angles with reasons.

nodes.label: Proving a parallelogram
nodes.description: Prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram by showing that one of the conditions holds on its sides, angles or diagonals, such as both pairs of opposite angles equal or the diagonals bisecting each other.

nodes.label: Rectangle and rhombus proofs
nodes.description: Prove, using congruent triangles, that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal and that the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other perpendicularly and bisect the interior angles, and prove that a quadrilateral is a rectangle or a rhombus.

nodes.label: Properties of a kite
nodes.description: Prove and apply the properties of a kite: one pair of opposite angles equal, the diagonal between the equal sides bisects the interior angles, and the diagonals intersect at right angles.

nodes.label: Naming special quadrilaterals
nodes.description: Name a quadrilateral from its properties, giving its most specific name and every name that applies (such as a square, rhombus, kite or trapezium), and use those properties to solve a problem such as finding an area.

nodes.label: Prove the mid-point theorem and use its converse
nodes.description: Prove that the line joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and equal to half its length, and use the converse to show that a line drawn through the mid-point of one side parallel to a second side bisects the third side.

nodes.label: Calculate lengths using mid-points
nodes.description: Calculate unknown lengths, including lengths given in terms of a variable, using the fact that the line joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is half the length of the third side.

$ABCD$ is a parallelogram with $AB\parallel DC$ and $AD\parallel BC$ . Show that: $AB=DC$ and $AD=BC$ $\hat{A}=\hat{C}$ and $\hat{B}=\hat{D}$ [figure]
Connect $AC$ to form $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$: Redraw the diagram and draw line $AC$ .
Use properties of parallel lines to indicate all equal angles on the diagram: On your diagram mark all the equal angles.

Prove $\triangle ABC\equiv\triangle CDA$: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$ : $\begin{aligned}\hat{A}_{2}&=\hat{C}_{3}&&\text{(alt}\angle\text{s;}AB\parallel DC\text{)}\\\hat{C}_{4}&=\hat{A}_{1}&&\text{(alt}\angle\text{s;}BC\parallel AD\text{)}\\AC&&&\text{(commonside)}\\\therefore\triangle ABC&\equiv\triangle CDA&&\text{(AAS)}\\\therefore AB&=CD\quad\text{and}\quad BC=DA\end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Opposite sides of a parallelogram have equal length. We have already shown ${\hat{A}}_{2}={\hat{C}}_{3}$ and ${\hat{A}}_{1}={\hat{C}}_{4}$ . Therefore, $\hat{A}=\hat{A}_{1}+\hat{A}_{2}=\hat{C}_{3}+\hat{C}_{4}=\hat{C}$ Furthermore, $\hat{B}=\hat{D}\enspace\left(\triangle ABC\equiv\triangle CDA\right)$ Therefore opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
Prove that if both pairs of opposite angles in a quadrilateral are equal, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram. [figure]

Find the relationship between $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$: In $WXYZ$ : $\begin{aligned}\hat{W}=\hat{Y}&=\hat{y}&&(\text{given})\\\hat{Z}=\hat{X}&=\hat{x}&&(\text{given})\\\hat{W}+\hat{X}+\hat{Y}+\hat{Z}&=360^{\circ}&&(\text{sumof}\angle\text{sinaquad})\\\therefore2\hat{x}+2\hat{y}&=360^{\circ}\\\therefore\hat{x}+\hat{y}&=180^{\circ}\\\hat{W}+\hat{Z}&=\hat{x}+\hat{y}\\&=180^{\circ}\end{aligned}$ But these are co-interior angles between lines $WX$ and $ZY$ . Therefore $WX\parallel ZY$ .

Find parallel lines: Similarly $\hat{W}+\hat{X}=180^{\circ}$ . These are co-interior angles between lines $XY$ and $WZ$ . Therefore $XY\parallel WZ$ . Both pairs of opposite sides of the quadrilateral are parallel, therefore $WXYZ$ is a parallelogram.
$PQRS$ is a rectangle. Prove that the diagonals are of equal length. [figure]

Prove $\triangle PSR\equiv\triangle QRS$: In $\triangle PSR$ and $\triangle QRS$ : $\begin{aligned}PS&=QR&&\text{(oppsidesofrectangle)}\\SR&&&\text{(commonside)}\\P\hat{S}R&=Q\hat{R}S=90^{\circ}&&\text{(}\angle\text{sofrectangle)}\\\therefore\triangle PSR&\equiv\triangle QRS&&\text{(RHS)}\\\text{Therefore}PR&=QS\end{aligned}$ The diagonals of a rectangle are of equal length.
$XYZT$ is a rhombus. Prove that: the diagonals bisect each other perpendicularly; the diagonals bisect the interior angles. [figure]

Prove $\triangle XTO\equiv\triangle ZTO$: $\begin{aligned}XT&=ZT&&(\text{sidesofrhombus})\\TO&&&(\text{commonside})\\XO&=OZ&&(\text{diagsofrhombus})\\\therefore\triangle XTO&\equiv\triangle ZTO&&(\text{SSS})\\\therefore\hat{O}_{1}&=\hat{O}_{4}\\\text{But}\hat{O}_{1}+\hat{O}_{4}&=180^{\circ}&&(\angle\text{sonastrline})\\\therefore\hat{O}_{1}&=\hat{O}_{4}=90^{\circ}\end{aligned}$ We can further conclude that $\hat{O}_{1}=\hat{O}_{2}=\hat{O}_{3}=\hat{O}_{4}=90^{\circ}$ . Therefore the diagonals bisect each other perpendicularly.

Use properties of congruent triangles to prove diagonals bisect interior angles: $\begin{aligned}\hat{X}_{2}&=\hat{Z}_{1}\quad(\triangle XTO\equiv\triangle ZTO)\\\text{and}\hat{X}_{2}&=\hat{Z}_{2}\quad(\text{alt}\angle\text{s};XT\parallel YZ)\\\therefore\hat{Z}_{1}&=\hat{Z}_{2}\end{aligned}$ Therefore diagonal $XZ$ bisects $\hat{Z}$ . Similarly, we can show that $XZ$ also bisects $\hat{X}$ ; and that diagonal $TY$ bisects $\hat{T}$ and $\hat{Y}$ . We conclude that the diagonals of a rhombus bisect the interior angles.
$ABCD$ is a kite with $AD=AB$ and $CD=CB$ . Prove that: $A\hat{D}C=A\hat{B}C$ Diagonal $AC$ bisects $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{C}$ [figure]

Prove $\triangle ADC\equiv\triangle ABC$: In $\triangle ADC$ and $\triangle ABC$ : $\begin{aligned}AD&=AB&&\text{(given)}\\CD&=CB&&\text{(given)}\\AC&&&\text{(commonside)}\\\therefore\triangle ADC&\equiv\triangle ABC&&\text{(SSS)}\\\therefore A\hat{D}C&=A\hat{B}C\end{aligned}$ Therefore one pair of opposite angles are equal in kite $ABCD$ .

Use properties of congruent triangles to prove $AC$ bisects $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{C}$: $\begin{aligned}\hat{A}_{1}&=\hat{A}_{2}\quad(\triangle ADC\equiv\triangle ABC)\\\text{and}\hat{C}_{1}&=\hat{C}_{2}\quad(\triangle ADC\equiv\triangle ABC)\end{aligned}$ Therefore diagonal $AC$ bisects $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{C}$ . We conclude that the diagonal between the equal sides of a kite bisects the two interior angles and is an axis of symmetry.
Prove that the diagonals of parallelogram $MNRS$ bisect one another at $P$ . [figure] Hint: Use congruency.
First number each angle on the given diagram: [figure] In $\triangle MNP$ and $\triangle RSP$ :

$\begin{aligned}\hat{M}_{1}&=\hat{R}_{1}\quad\text{(alt }\angle\text{s; }MN\parallel SR\text{)}\\\hat{P}_{1}&=\hat{P}_{3}\quad\text{(vert opp }\angle\text{s }=\text{)}\\MN&=RS\text{ (opp sides of }\parallel\text{m)}\end{aligned}$
Therefore $\triangle MNP\equiv\triangle RSP$ (AAS). Now we know that $MP=RP$ and therefore $P$ is the mid-point of $MR$ . Similarly, in $\triangle MSP$ and $\triangle RNP$ :

$\begin{aligned}\hat{M}_{2}&=\hat{R}_{2}\quad\text{(alt }\angle\text{s; }MS\parallel NR\text{)}\\\hat{P}_{4}&=\hat{P}_{2}\quad\text{(vert opp }\angle\text{s }=\text{)}\\MS&=RN\text{ (opp sides of }\parallel\text{m)}\end{aligned}$
Therefore $\triangle MSP\equiv\triangle RNP$ (AAS). Now we know that $NP=SP$ and therefore $P$ is the mid-point of $NS$ . Therefore the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
$ABCD$ is a quadrilateral. Diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $T$ . $AC=BD$ , $AT=TC$ , $DT=TB$ . Prove that: [figure] $ABCD$ is a parallelogram
$AT=TC$ (given) $\therefore DB$ bisects $AC$ at $T$ and $DT=TB$ (given) $\therefore AC$ bisects $DB$ at $T$ therefore quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a parallelogram (diag of $\parallel$ m)
$ABCD$ is a quadrilateral. Diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $T$ . $AC=BD$ , $AT=TC$ , $DT=TB$ . Prove that: [figure] $ABCD$ is a rectangle
$AC=BD$ (given). Therefore $ABCD$ is a rectangle (diags of rectangle).
Use the sketch of quadrilateral $ABCD$ to prove the diagonals of a kite are perpendicular to each other. [figure]
First number the angles: [figure] In $\triangle ADO$ and $\triangle ABO$ :

$\begin{aligned}AD&=AB&&\text{(given)}\\AO&&&\text{(commonside)}\\B\hat{A}O&=D\hat{A}O&&\text{(given)}\\\therefore\triangle ADO&\equiv\triangle ABO&&\text{(SAS)}\\\therefore A\hat{B}O&=A\hat{D}O\end{aligned}$
In $\triangle ADB$ :

$\begin{aligned}\text{let}\hat{A}_{1}&=\hat{A}_{2}=t\\\text{andlet}A\hat{D}O&=A\hat{B}O=p\\2t+2p&=180^{\circ}\quad\text{(sumof}\angle\text{sin}\triangle\text{)}\\\therefore t+p&=90^{\circ}\end{aligned}$
Next we note that:
$\begin{aligned}\hat{O}_{1}&=A\hat{B}O+\hat{A}_{1}\quad\text{(ext}\angle\text{of}\triangle\text{)}\\\hat{O}_{1}&=p+t\\&=90^{\circ}\\\therefore AC&\perp BD\end{aligned}$
Therefore the diagonals of a kite are perpendicular to each other.
Explain why quadrilateral $WXYZ$ is a kite. Write down all the properties of quadrilateral $WXYZ$ . [figure]

[figure] Quadrilateral $WXYZ$ is a kite because is has two pairs of adjacent sides that are equal in length. Diagonal between equal sides bisects the other diagonal: $WP=PY$ . One pair of opposite angles are equal: $\hat{W}_{1}=\hat{Y}_{1}$ . Diagonal between equal sides bisects the interior angles and is an axis of symmetry: $\hat{X}_{1}=\hat{X}_{2}$ . Diagonals intersect at $90^{\circ}$ : $WY\perp PX$ .
$\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle PSR$ are equilateral triangles. Prove that $PQRS$ is a rhombus. [figure]

We are given two equilateral triangles, therefore in $\triangle PSR$ : $PS=SR=PR$ and in $\triangle PQR$ : $PQ=QR=PR$ . But $PR$ is a common side and so $PR=PS=SR=PQ=QR$ . claims.claim: An angle is formed when two straight lines meet at a point, which is also known as a vertex.
An angle is labelled with a caret on a letter, for example B̂.
An angle can also be labelled according to the line segments that make up the angle, for example CB̂A or AB̂C.
The symbol ∠ is a short way of writing 'angle' in geometry.
Angles are measured in degrees, denoted by the symbol °, a small circle raised above the text, similar to an exponent.
An acute angle is an angle greater than 0° and less than 90°.
A right angle is an angle equal to 90°.
An obtuse angle is an angle greater than 90° and less than 180°.
A straight angle is an angle equal to 180°.
A reflex angle is an angle greater than 180° and less than 360°.
Adjacent angles are angles that share a vertex and a common side.
Vertically opposite angles are angles opposite each other when two lines intersect.
Vertically opposite angles share a vertex and are equal.
Supplementary angles are two angles that add up to 180°.
Complementary angles are two angles that add up to 90°.
A revolution is the sum of all angles around a point.
The angles around a point (a revolution) add up to 360°; for the four angles formed by two intersecting lines, â + b̂ + ĉ + d̂ = 360°.
Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary.
Two lines intersect if they cross each other at a point.
Parallel lines are always the same distance apart.
Parallel lines are denoted in a diagram by arrow symbols.
In writing, two vertical lines (∥) are used to indicate that two lines are parallel.
A transversal line intersects two or more parallel lines.
Interior angles are angles that lie in between the parallel lines; interior means inside.
Exterior angles are angles that lie outside the parallel lines; exterior means outside.
Corresponding angles are angles on the same side of the lines and the same side of the transversal.
If the lines are parallel, the corresponding angles formed by a transversal are equal.
Co-interior angles are angles that lie in between the lines and on the same side of the transversal.
If the lines are parallel, co-interior angles are supplementary (they add up to 180°).
Alternate interior angles are interior angles that lie inside the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.
If the lines are parallel, the alternate interior angles are equal.
If two lines are intersected by a transversal such that corresponding angles are equal, then the two lines are parallel.
If two lines are intersected by a transversal such that alternate interior angles are equal, then the two lines are parallel.
If two lines are intersected by a transversal such that co-interior angles are supplementary, then the two lines are parallel.
EF written for lines means the line through points E and F.
The notation EF with an overline (\overline{EF}) means the line segment from point E to point F.
To find unknown angles in a diagram with parallel lines, use the properties of parallel lines to find all equal angles, then redraw the diagram and mark all the equal angles.
Start the working by stating the given information with the reason 'given', for example AB ∥ CD (given); every following line of working then carries its reason in brackets.
To find an angle that is an alternate angle to a known angle, set it equal and give the reason 'alt ∠s; AB ∥ CD', for example x̂ = 60°.
To find an angle that is co-interior to a known angle, write that the two add up to 180° with the reason 'co-int ∠s; AB ∥ CD', then solve, for example ŷ + 160° = 180° so ŷ = 20°.
To find an angle that is vertically opposite a known angle, set the two equal and give the reason 'vertopp ∠s =', for example p̂ = ŷ.
To find an angle that corresponds to a known angle, set the two equal and give the reason 'corresp ∠s; AB ∥ CD', for example r̂ = 160°.
To find an angle that lies with other angles on a straight line, write that the angles add up to 180° with the reason '∠s on a str line', then solve, for example ŝ + x̂ + 90° = 180° so ŝ = 30°.
To test whether two lines are parallel, suppose they are, so that a pair of corresponding angles would be equal, and compare the sizes of those angles.
If the corresponding angles that would be equal for parallel lines are not equal (here p̂ = 20° but ŝ = 30°), conclude that the lines are not parallel (EF is not parallel to CG).
A triangle is a three-sided polygon.
Triangles can be classified according to their sides as equilateral, isosceles or scalene.
Triangles can also be classified according to their angles as acute-angled, obtuse-angled or right-angled.
The notation △ABC refers to a triangle with vertices labelled A, B and C.
A scalene triangle has all sides and angles different.
An isosceles triangle has two sides equal in length.
In an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite the equal sides are also equal.
An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal in length and all three angles equal.
An acute triangle has each of its three interior angles less than 90°.
An obtuse triangle has one interior angle greater than 90°.
A right-angled triangle has one interior angle equal to 90°.
Properties from the classification by sides and by angles can be combined in one triangle; for example, an obtuse isosceles triangle and a right-angled isosceles triangle are possible.
In the interior-angles Investigation, the three angles cut from a triangle are placed along a ruler (a straight line), with the hint to think about the sum of angles on a straight line.
The angles in a triangle add up to 180°.
Two triangles are congruent if one fits exactly over the other.
Congruent triangles have equal corresponding angles and sides.
To determine whether two triangles are congruent, it is not necessary to check every side and every angle.
Congruency is indicated using the symbol ≡.

RHS (also written 90° HS: 90°, hypotenuse, side): if the hypotenuse and one side of a right-angled triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and the corresponding side of another right-angled triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.
SSS (side, side, side): if three sides of a triangle are equal in length to the corresponding sides of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.

SAS (also written S∠S: side, angle, side): if two sides and the included angle of a triangle are equal to the corresponding two sides and included angle of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.
AAS (also written ∠∠S: angle, angle, side): if one side and two angles of a triangle are equal to the corresponding one side and two angles of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.
The order of letters when labelling congruent triangles is very important.
Writing △ABC ≡ △DEF indicates that Â = D̂, B̂ = Ê, Ĉ = F̂, AB = DE, AC = DF and BC = EF; the letters are matched in order.
The symbol ≅ may also be used to show that two triangles are congruent; it is the internationally recognised symbol for congruency.
Two triangles are similar if one triangle is a scaled version of the other.
Similar triangles have corresponding angles equal in measure and the ratios of their corresponding sides in proportion.
Similar triangles have the same shape but different scales.
Congruent triangles are similar triangles, but not all similar triangles are congruent.
Similarity of two triangles is indicated using the symbol |||.
AAA (angle, angle, angle): if all three pairs of corresponding angles of two triangles are equal, then the triangles are similar.
To show similarity by AAA, state the three pairs of equal corresponding angles (Â = D̂, B̂ = Ê, Ĉ = F̂) and conclude △ABC ||| △DEF.
SSS (side, side, side): if all three pairs of corresponding sides of two triangles are in proportion, then the triangles are similar.
To show similarity by SSS, show that MN/RS = ML/RT = NL/ST, and conclude △MNL ||| △RST.
The order of letters for similar triangles is very important; similar triangles must always be labelled in corresponding order.
△MNL ||| △RST is correct, but △MNL ||| △RTS is incorrect.
The symbol ∼ may also be used to show that two triangles are similar; it is the internationally recognised symbol for similarity.
Theorem of Pythagoras: if △ABC is right-angled with B̂ = 90°, then b² = a² + c².
Converse of the theorem of Pythagoras: if b² = a² + c², then △ABC is right-angled with B̂ = 90°.

To find an unknown angle in a triangle, write the sum of the three angles equal to 180° with the reason (sum of angles in a triangle), substitute the known angles and solve; for example 90° + 35° + Ê = 180°, so Ê = 55°.

To determine whether two triangles are congruent, name the two triangles, list pairs of equal angles and sides each with its reason (given or proved), and conclude the congruence with the rule used, here AAS, writing △CDE ≡ △CBA in corresponding order.
To find an unknown side of a right-angled triangle, write the theorem of Pythagoras for that triangle (CE² = DE² + CD²), substitute the known lengths (5² = 3² + x²) and solve (x² = 16, so x = 4).
To find an unknown angle in the second triangle, apply the sum of angles in a triangle again: B̂ + Â + ŷ = 180°, so 90° + 55° + ŷ = 180° and ŷ = 35°.
Once the triangles are proved congruent, use the congruence to equate corresponding sides: since △CDE ≡ △CBA, CE = CA, so z = 5.
In worked solutions, each statement is followed by its reason in brackets, such as (given), (proved), (sum of angles in a triangle), (Pythagoras) or (AAS).
A quadrilateral is a closed shape consisting of four straight line segments.
The interior angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees.
A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
Both pairs of opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal in length.
Both pairs of opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
To prove the properties of parallelogram ABCD (AB parallel to DC, AD parallel to BC), redraw the diagram and draw the diagonal AC to form two triangles.
Use the properties of parallel lines to indicate all equal angles on the diagram before proving the triangles congruent.
In the parallelogram proof the equal angles come from alternate angles between parallel lines (A2 = C3 because AB is parallel to DC), and each statement in the proof is given a reason in brackets.
Triangles ABC and CDA are shown congruent by AAS (two pairs of alternate angles and the common side AC), so AB = CD and BC = DA.
Opposite sides of a parallelogram have equal length.
To show angle A equals angle C in a parallelogram, add the two parts of each angle: A = A1 + A2 = C3 + C4 = C, using the equal alternate angles already found.
Angle B equals angle D in a parallelogram because triangles ABC and CDA are congruent.
Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if both pairs of opposite sides are equal.
A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if both pairs of opposite angles are equal.
A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if its diagonals bisect each other.
A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if one pair of opposite sides are both equal and parallel.
To prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, show that any one of the listed conditions on its sides, angles or diagonals holds.
To prove that a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite angles equal is a parallelogram, let the equal angles be x and y and use the sum of the angles in a quadrilateral, 360 degrees.
From 2x + 2y = 360 degrees it follows that x + y = 180 degrees, so each pair of adjacent angles (such as W and Z) adds up to 180 degrees.
Adjacent angles adding up to 180 degrees are co-interior angles, which shows the lines are parallel (W + Z = 180 degrees gives WX parallel to ZY).
Once both pairs of opposite sides are shown parallel, the quadrilateral WXYZ is a parallelogram.
A rectangle is a parallelogram that has all four angles equal to 90 degrees.
A rectangle has all the properties of a parallelogram.
The diagonals of a rectangle are equal in length.
To prove the diagonals of rectangle PQRS are equal, show triangles PSR and QRS congruent using PS = QR (opposite sides of a rectangle), the common side SR, and the right angles of the rectangle.
The diagonals of a rectangle are of equal length (PR = QS).
A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides of equal length.
A rhombus has all the properties of a parallelogram.

To prove the diagonals of rhombus XYZT bisect each other perpendicularly, show triangles XTO and ZTO congruent by SSS, using XT = ZT (sides of a rhombus), the common side TO and XO = OZ (diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other).
From the congruent triangles O1 = O4, and since angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees, O1 = O4 = 90 degrees.
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other perpendicularly.

To prove the diagonals of a rhombus bisect the interior angles, use the congruent triangles together with alternate angles between parallel sides (X2 = Z1 from the congruent triangles and X2 = Z2 from XT parallel to YZ, so Z1 = Z2).
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect the interior angles.
A rhombus has all sides equal in length.
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect both pairs of opposite angles.
To prove a parallelogram is a rhombus, show any one of the following: all sides are equal in length, the diagonals intersect at right angles, or the diagonals bisect the interior angles.
A parallelogram is a rhombus if its diagonals intersect at right angles.
A parallelogram is a rhombus if its diagonals bisect the interior angles.
A kite is a quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent sides equal.
In a kite, one pair of opposite angles are equal (the angles between unequal sides).
In a kite, the diagonal between the equal sides bisects the interior angles and is an axis of symmetry.
In a kite, the diagonal between the equal sides bisects the other diagonal.
The diagonals of a kite intersect at 90 degrees.
To prove the properties of kite ABCD (AD = AB and CD = CB), show triangles ADC and ABC congruent by SSS, using the two given pairs of equal sides and the common side AC.
One pair of opposite angles are equal in a kite (angle ADC equals angle ABC).
To prove that diagonal AC bisects angles A and C, use the congruent triangles ADC and ABC: A1 = A2 and C1 = C2.
The diagonal between the equal sides of a kite bisects the two interior angles and is an axis of symmetry.
A square is a rhombus with all four interior angles equal to 90 degrees.
A square is also defined as a rectangle with all four sides equal in length.
A square has all the properties of a rhombus.
The diagonals of a square are equal in length.
The diagonals of a square bisect both pairs of interior opposite angles, so all the angles they make are 45 degrees.
To prove a parallelogram is a square, show that it is a rhombus (all four sides of equal length) with interior angles equal to 90 degrees.
A trapezium is a quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides parallel.
A trapezium is sometimes called a trapezoid.
